questions.stem: What forms after successful pollination to reach the ovum?

options.text: A pollen tube growing from the pollen grain
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The style already exists; the tube grows through it.
The ovary is a flower part, not a tube product.
Seeds form after fertilisation, not at pollination.

questions.stem: Along which route does the pollen tube grow?

options.text: Out of the petal to a pollinator
options.explanation: Pollinators carried the grain; the tube works alone now.

options.text: Down the style toward the ovary
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Up the stigma into the air
options.explanation: The tube grows inward, not outward.

options.text: Along the filament to the anther
options.explanation: The anther is the male part that made the pollen.

questions.stem: What exactly fuses during fertilisation in a flower?

options.explanation: One male nucleus fuses with one female nucleus.
Those are structures, not fusing cells.

options.text: The pollen nucleus fusing with the ovum nucleus
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The whole pollen grain and the stigma
options.explanation: The stigma only received the grain.

questions.stem: What single cell results when the two plant nuclei merge?

options.explanation: The tube formed before fusion.
The ovule develops into a seed after fertilisation.
Fruit forms from surrounding flower parts, later.
Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: Why must the pollen nucleus travel down a tube rather than swimming to the ovum?

options.text: The route runs through solid style tissue, so the tube delivers the nucleus to the ovary
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Nectar is a reward; there is no swim channel.
Wind was the courier outside; inside the tube does the work.

options.text: The ovum crawls up to meet pollen
options.explanation: The ovum stays put in the ovary.

questions.stem: State where the pollen tube grows and what it delivers.
questions.modelAnswer: The pollen tube grows down the style and delivers the male nucleus into the ovary.

questions.stem: State the definition of fertilisation in plants.
questions.modelAnswer: Fertilisation is the moment the pollen nucleus merges with the ovum nucleus, creating a zygote.

questions.stem: Explain why pollination and fertilisation are not the same event.
questions.modelAnswer: Pollination is pollen landing on the stigma, while fertilisation happens later when the nuclei fuse inside the ovary after the tube's growth.

questions.stem: A chemical blocks style tissue growth so no tube can form. Predict the consequence for reproduction.
questions.modelAnswer: The pollen nucleus could not reach the ovum, so fertilisation would fail and no seed would form.

questions.stem: What does the ovule become after fertilisation?

options.explanation: The ovary is where the ovule sat; it does not become one.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The fruit forms from the surrounding flower parts.
The tube already served its delivery role.

questions.stem: Which structures develop into the fruit?

options.explanation: Pollen delivered the male nucleus and is spent.
The surrounding ovary tissues form the fruit wall.

options.text: The flower tissues that wrap around the ovule
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Ovules become seeds inside the fruit.

questions.stem: Why do fruits help the plant's offspring?

options.text: They feed the seed while it grows
options.explanation: The seed carries its own food store.

options.text: They attract pollinators to the flower
options.explanation: Pollination already happened.
Fertilisation is complete before fruit growth.

options.text: They provide a mechanism for seed dispersal away from the parent
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: A fox eats berries and walks kilometres before its droppings land. What service did the fox provide?

options.text: Seed dispersal, moving the seeds far from the parent plant
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
The fox ate fruit, not pollen.
Fertilisation happened in the flower, long before.
Germination starts after dispersal, once deposited.

questions.stem: Which fruit adaptation suits hitching a ride on an animal's coat?

options.explanation: Stones protect seeds; they do not grip fur.

options.text: Sticky hooks that catch in fur
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Sweet flesh eaten for the flesh itself
options.explanation: Sweet flesh suits droppings dispersal, not hooks.
Colour attracts eaters; hooks do the attaching.

questions.stem: State what the ovule and the surrounding flower parts become after fertilisation.
questions.modelAnswer: The ovule becomes a seed, and the flower parts that wrapped it become the fruit.

questions.stem: Name two fruit dispersal mechanisms given in the lesson.
questions.modelAnswer: Fruits can be eaten by animals that disperse seeds in droppings, or carry sticky hooks that catch in animal fur.

questions.stem: Explain why seed dispersal benefits the next generation of plants.
questions.modelAnswer: Dispersal moves seeds away from the parent plant, so seedlings do not compete with the parent or with each other for light, water and minerals.

questions.stem: A meadow plant makes hooked fruits while a neighbour makes sweet fleshy fruits. Assign each its dispersal agent.
questions.modelAnswer: The hooked fruits hitch on passing animals' fur, and the fleshy fruits are eaten by animals that disperse the seeds in their droppings.
